Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Therefore [F2] gives neighborhoods $U,V$ and a unique $C^k$ function $\psi$ with the stated equivalence and derivative formula. Splitting that combined derivative into its $t$ and $x$ blocks gives the two displayed identities.

Differentiating $g(t,x,\psi(t,x))=0$ in the $t$ direction using [F3] gives $g_t+g_z\psi_t=0$; multiplying by $g_z^{-1}$ gives $\psi_t=-g_z^{-1}g_t$. Differentiating in each $x$ direction gives $g_x+g_z\psi_x=0$, hence $\psi_x=-g_z^{-1}g_x$.

The map $(t,x)\mapsto (t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$, so [F3] applied to its composition with the $C^k$ map $f$ shows $F(t,x)=f(t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$. Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Fix any $(t,x)\in K$, put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$, and set $\delta=z-z_*$. Since $g(t,x,z_*)=0$, [F2] applied to each component along the segment from $z_*$ to $z$ gives $g(t,x,z)=G_*(t,x)\delta+R$. Each component remainder is at most $(\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$; aggregating the $m$ components gives $\|R\|_2\le(\sqrt m\,\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$.

The common lower singular-value bound gives $\|G_*(t,x)\delta\|_2\ge\gamma\|\delta\|_2$. Using [F3] in the form $\|G_*(t,x)\delta+R\|_2\ge\|G_*(t,x)\delta\|_2-\|R\|_2$, we obtain $\|g(t,x,z)\|_2\ge(\gamma-(\sqrt m\,\Lambda/2)\|\delta\|_2)\|\delta\|_2$. If $\Lambda>0$, $\|\delta\|_2<\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$ makes the parenthesis at least $\gamma/2$; if $\Lambda=0$, it equals $\gamma$. In either case it is at least $\gamma/2$, with the same constants for every $(t,x)\in K$.
Dividing the inequality in step 2.1 by $\gamma/2>0$ proves the asserted residual-to-state estimate for every candidate in the branch ball.

The procedure makes at most $N$ correction calls, at most $N$ accepted updates, and at most $N+1$ explicit outer residual evaluations. It returns a stated residual, singular-Jacobian, invalid-trial or budget status. Termination is in the exact-arithmetic model where residual and Jacobian evaluations, domain decisions and correction calls return in finite time. No convergence, tolerance-attainment or backend complexity claim follows.

Let $f,g$ define a regular index-one DAE and let $U\times V$ be a selected local branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], so $g(t,x,z)=0$ is equivalent to $z=\psi(t,x)$ there. Input $t_0,x_0$, a seed $z_{\mathrm{seed}}\in V$, an algebraic residual tolerance $\varepsilon_a\ge0$, and a finite Newton-correction budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. If $(t_0,x_0)\notin U$, $g(t_0,x_0,\cdot)$ is undefined at the seed, or dimensions do not match, return invalid-input.

Call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on the square residual $G(z)=g(t_0,x_0,z)$, with initial value $z_{\mathrm{seed}}$, tolerance $\varepsilon_a$, and budget $N$, restricting evaluations to the chart's open $z$-domain. If it reports root, reevaluate $G(z_0)$ once: if that residual is exactly zero, return $(x_0,z_0,\texttt{exact-consistent})$; otherwise return $(x_0,z_0,\texttt{approximate-consistent})$ and its norm. Map singular-jacobian, invalid-trial, and iteration-budget-exhausted to the corresponding initialization statuses and return the last valid iterate.

The procedure makes no arbitrary-start convergence claim. approximate-consistent records a residual bound; it is not relabeled as exact consistency. Under the index-one branch hypotheses an exact consistent value exists locally, by [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], but the finite Newton budget may fail to find it.

The solve has $m$ algebraic unknowns. Record residual queries, Jacobian assemblies and correction solves separately. Their costs depend on the chosen backend.

Input $f,g$, a constant grid $t_n=t_0+nh$ with $h>0$ and $N_t\in\mathbb N$, an initial pair $(X_0,Z_0)$, and a selected open tube $\mathcal T\subset\Omega$ inside the local branch chart of [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], where $g(t,x,z)=0$ is equivalent to $z=\psi(t,x)$. For each time $t$, write $\mathcal T_t=\{(X,Z):(t,X,Z)\in\mathcal T\}$ for the open state slice used as the Newton evaluation domain. Also input positive residual tolerances $\eta_d,\eta_a$, a finite Newton-correction budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and an initial algebraic-residual bound $\eta_{a,0}\ge0$. Return invalid-grid if $h\le0$ or $N_t=0$, and invalid-input for incompatible dimensions, data outside the function domains, or $(X_0,Z_0)\notin\mathcal T_{t_0}$. Compute the starting algebraic residual once; return inconsistent-initial-data if $\|g(t_0,X_0,Z_0)\|_2>\eta_{a,0}$.

For $n=1,\ldots,N_t$, form the coupled update residual

$$
R_n(X,Z)=\bigl(X-X_{n-1}-h f(t_n,X,Z),\ g(t_n,X,Z)\bigr)
$$

and the scaled square residual

$$
\mathcal R_n(X,Z)=\left(\frac{X-X_{n-1}-h f(t_n,X,Z)}{h\eta_d},\ \frac{g(t_n,X,Z)}{\eta_a}\right).
$$

Use $(X_{n-1},Z_{n-1})$ as the Newton seed. Before calling Newton, if $(X_{n-1},Z_{n-1})\notin\mathcal T_{t_n}$, return invalid-trial with the already computed prefix. Otherwise call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on $\mathcal R_n$ with residual tolerance $1$, budget $B$, and $\mathcal T_{t_n}$ as its evaluation domain. If the returned status is root and the candidate lies in $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, reevaluate $R_n$ once to retain both unscaled residuals, then append the candidate. Then there are neighborhoods $U$ of $(t_*,x_*)$ and $V$ of $z_*$, and a unique $C^k$ map $\psi:U\to V$, such that, for $(t,x)\in U$ and $z\in V$,

$$
g(t,x,z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\psi(t,x).
$$

Its derivatives satisfy

$$
\psi_t=-g_z^{-1}g_t,\qquad \psi_x=-g_z^{-1}g_x,
$$

with the derivatives of $g$ evaluated at $(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. The reduced vector field $F(t,x)=f(t,x,\psi(t,x))$ is $C^k$ on $U$. Thus solutions of the DAE that stay in this selected chart are exactly solutions of $x'=F(t,x)$ paired with $z=\psi(t,x)$.

Let $K$ be a compact set of base points $(t,x)$ in a selected branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], and put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$. $$

$$
\|z-z_*\|_2\le \frac{2}{\gamma}\|g(t,x,z)\|_2.
$$

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

Fix a semi-explicit presentation $x'=f(t,x,z)$, $0=g(t,x,z)$ as in [[def-semi-explicit-index-one-dae-and-consistent-initial-data]] and a sufficiently differentiable consistent local solution. Differentiate the algebraic constraint along the differential equation, substituting $x'=f(t,x,z)$ and any previously obtained derivative relations at each stage. The **differentiation index in this convention** is the least positive integer $k$ for which the original constraint and its first $k$ differentiated equations locally determine $z$ and $z'$, with the equation for the highest derivative of $z$ having an invertible square Jacobian on a neighborhood of the solution. If no such finite $k$ exists, this local index is undefined. This convention counts through the first derivative of the algebraic variables and is local to the fixed presentation; it is not a universal index theory for arbitrary implicit systems.

If $g_z$ is invertible, one differentiation gives

$$
g_t+g_x f+g_z z'=0,
$$

which determines $z'$, so the index is one. If $g_z$ is singular, the index must be checked from the actual differentiated equations; no index-one conclusion follows from this definition alone.

The constant functions $x(t)=0,z(t)=0$ satisfy both equations, so the system has a solution with the consistent initial pair $(0,0)$. The three boundary calculations above concern only this fixed index-two system and imply no index-one numerical guarantee.
